final_text: But the hardships of Lowood eased. Spring arrived—she was already here, in fact. The frosts of winter had ended, the snows had melted, the cutting winds had softened. My wretched feet, raw and swollen to the point of lameness from the sharp January air, began to heal and recover under the gentler breath of April. The nights and mornings no longer froze the blood in our veins with their arctic cold. We could now bear the play hour in the garden. Sometimes on a sunny day it even began to feel pleasant, and a green tinge spread over those brown beds, freshening daily, suggesting that Hope had walked through them in the night and left brighter traces of her steps each morning. Flowers peeked out among the leaves: snowdrops, crocuses, purple auriculas, and golden-eyed pansies. On Thursday afternoons, which were half-holidays, we now went on walks and found still sweeter flowers opening along the roadsides and under the hedges.

final_text: April gave way to May—a bright, clear May of blue skies, calm sunshine, and soft western or southern breezes that filled its days from start to finish. The greenery surged with new life. Lowood shook out its foliage. It became all green, all flowers. Its great elms, ashes, and oaks, which had been mere skeletons, were restored to majestic life. Woodland plants sprang up thickly in every hollow. Countless varieties of moss filled the shadowy places, and the wild primroses made a strange ground-level sunshine with their pale gold gleam. I have seen them shining in overshadowed spots like scatterings of the gentlest light. All this I enjoyed often and freely, unwatched and nearly alone. For this unusual freedom, there was a cause, which I must now explain.

final_text: My favorite seat was a smooth, broad stone rising white and dry from the very middle of the stream, reachable only by wading through the water—a feat I accomplished barefoot. She was a shrewd, observant person whose company I enjoyed, partly because she was witty and original, and partly because she had a manner that put me at ease. She was also tolerant of my faults, never curbing or censoring anything I said. She had a talent for storytelling, I for analysis; she liked to inform, I to question. Everything within their boundary of rock and heath felt like a prison yard, the bounds of an exile. I traced the white road winding around the base of one mountain and vanishing into a pass between two others. How I longed to follow it! I remembered the time I had traveled that very road in a coach, descending that hill at twilight.
